Hey CodinGamer! Your contribution has unfortunately not been moderated on time and will temporarily be removed from the system... But no worries! You can republish it anytime to give it another chance! :)

Consider shortening the problem statement, for example:

- Omitting the worked example, since it appears as the first test case.
- Telling players to choose 1/ceil(q/p) is fine, but they can work out the remainder themselves.
- Omitting description of GCD, and simplifying unnecessary mathematical language.

E.g. (I threw this into ChatGPT, feel free to modify as you see fit):

An <<Egyptian fraction>> expresses a positive rational number as a <<sum of distinct unit fractions>>. A unit fraction takes the form 1/[[k]] for a positive integer [[k]]. One way to find such a representation is the <<Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy algorithm>>, which repeatedly chooses the largest unit fraction that does not exceed the remaining fraction.

For a fraction [[p]]/[[q]] (where 0 < [[p]]/[[q]] < 1), choose the unit fraction 1/ceil([[q]]/[[p]]), subtract it from [[p]]/[[q]], and reduce the remainder to its lowest terms using the greatest common divisor (GCD). Repeat until the remainder is a unit fraction.

To handle [[p]]/[[q]] ≥ 1, first greedily choose 1/1, 1/2, 1/3, and so on, stopping before the next unit fraction would make the sum exceed [[p]]/[[q]]. Then apply the algorithm stated above to the remaining fraction.

Given positive integers [[p]] and [[q]], find the Egyptian fraction representation of [[p]]/[[q]] using this algorithm. Output the denominators of the unit fractions in ascending order.

Comment: I’m waiting for the optimisation puzzle!
And I discovered that while/else works in Python.

Why not an optimisation puzzle about this theme, where you must minimise the number of fractions and/or their greatest denominator?
This puzzle will be an introduction to the optimisation puzzle.

Goal
* Please correct the typo (it appears twice): Egyption => Egyptian.

* Please correct the typo: Egyptan => Egyptian.

* The explanation on the modified version of Fibonacci's algorithm is a bit confusing. Consider rewriting it as follows:

As stated above, Fibonacci's algorithm only works for rational numbers between 0 and 1. In the modified version of Fibonacci's algorithm, start by choosing the unit fractions 1/1, 1/2, 1/3, ..., in order, until adding the next unit fraction would exceed [[p]]/[[q]]. Then use the original Fibonacci's algorithm to determine the unit fractions required to represent the remaining fraction.

* Consider removing the link to "harmonic number" if knowledge of this concept isn't strictly necessary for solving the puzzle.

Output
* Please format all instances of "/", "1/", "+" and "1/1" as {{constants}}.

* Please format "a" and "b" as [[variables]].

Cases
* Validator 2's name is missing.

* Is there a reason why Pair 8 is placed at the end rather than earlier?

* Please add a pair of cases between Pair 3 and Pair 4, where 200 ≤ p, q ≤ 10000 and p / q can be directly reduced to 1 / k.

* If possible, please add a pair of cases where p > q, gcd(p, q) > 1, and p and q are 6-digit numbers.

Thanks.

Thank you, the suggested changes are done.

BTW: Saving changes that involves re-executing the test cases hangs - test cases are tested, then "Submitting" is shown for a long time. Only a page reload helps afterwards. It's been like that for a long time. Pretty annoying.
Yes, this would be possible. But let's get this published first.
It states "For all initial and intermediate fractions p/q", so yes, the initial values are much smaller, but the intermediate values (before reduction) can be that large.

Thanks, I have updated the text. I have changed the last sentence to make it clear that we want the unit fractions with denominators in ascending order as a sum, not just the denominators in ascending order.
Nice, thank you! Please also update your constraints since your largest values of p and/or q do not seem to exceed 2 million (way smaller than your described constraints).
The constraints are imposed on "intermediate" fractions too (though I'm not sure whether "intermediate" is the correct word to use).

I missed the "intermediate" fractions, but it would still make sense to update [[p]] at least?

Am good either way.
I haven't solved the puzzle yet, so I don't know whether any of the fractions has a large [[p]] before simplification.

The gist is that in all occurring fractions (initial and during calculations), p and q can be stored/processed as 64-bit integers, so it is not necessary to use an arbitrary-size integer library for the solution.
